title: DevSecOps
summary: DevSecOps is the practice of building security work into the software delivery pipeline so that checks run continuously and automatically rather than in a review gate at the end. It redistributes responsibility: developers fix findings in the tools they already use, platform teams expose secure defaults and reusable components, and security engineers build the tests, policies and paved roads. In practice it means dependency and secret scanning on every commit, checks on infrastructure as code, signed build artefacts, and automated policy that can block a release once an agreed threshold is crossed. The common mistake is bolting a scanner onto the pipeline and calling the work finished: without triage ownership, agreed severity thresholds and fast feedback, teams learn to ignore the output. DevSecOps changes who does security work and when it happens, not just which tool runs.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-218: Secure Software Development Framework

beginner.definition: DevSecOps means adding security work to the way software is built and released. Instead of checking security at the very end, teams run small checks all the time. Everyone who builds the software shares some responsibility for keeping it safe.
beginner.whyItMatters: Software changes every day, and a check that happens once a year cannot keep up. Fixing a problem early is far cheaper than fixing it after release. Automatic checks also give fast feedback, so developers can correct issues while the work is still fresh. When security is a last gate, releases are delayed and arguments start. Shared responsibility helps the whole team care about safety, not just one group.
howItWorks: Developers commit small changes often, and automatic tools check every single change.
The tools look for known weak components, secret keys and unsafe settings.
Results appear where developers already work, so they can fix them quickly.
The team agrees which findings block a release and which are only recorded.
Build artefacts are signed and stored, so only trusted versions are used.
Security engineers build safe defaults and reusable parts that others can copy.
beginner.example: Think of a busy restaurant kitchen during dinner service. Instead of one health inspector visiting once a year, the cooks check things as they work. They test temperatures, wash hands and label food. A small problem is spotted in minutes rather than months. The head chef sets the standards and provides the right tools, and everyone follows them. If the kitchen waited for one yearly visit, a single bad evening could make many people ill. Software teams work the same way when they check security as they build, not only at the end.
takeaways: Run security checks on every change, not once before release.
Agree which findings must block a release, or people will ignore them.
Security teams should provide safe defaults, not only reports.

objectives: Explain what DevSecOps means and how it changes when security work happens.
Describe the automated checks that commonly run in a delivery pipeline.
Explain how agreed thresholds decide which findings block a release.
Identify the operational failures that turn pipeline scanning into noise.
Describe the shared responsibilities of developers, platform teams and security.
